part2.intro: Three young people talk about their favourite time of the year.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Mia
texts.text: Winter is the best time of year for me. My birthday is on the twentieth of December, so it's always close to Christmas and I get lots of presents! Every January my family goes skiing in the mountains for a week. I love it, but it gets dark at about four o'clock in the afternoon, so we can't ski for very long each day. I don't mind the cold weather – I feel tired and lazy when it's hot.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Kenji
texts.text: I love summer because the school holidays are two months long. Every July I fly to Japan to stay with my grandparents. My grandfather wakes me up at five o'clock in the morning and we go fishing on the lake before breakfast. It's quiet and beautiful at that time of day. In the evenings we sometimes watch fireworks. I'm always sad when it's time to come home at the end of August.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Lan
texts.text: My favourite season is autumn. In September the new school year starts and I see all my friends again after the long summer holiday. There's also the Mid-Autumn Festival. On that night, children carry lanterns in the street and look at the moon. The week before, I help my mum make moon cakes in our kitchen. It takes the whole weekend, but it's great fun.

items.q: Whose birthday is in their favourite season?
Who enjoys doing something very early in the day?

Who travels to another country every year?

Who feels unhappy when their favourite time ends?

part3.title: The boy who loves clocks
part3.text:
Most teenagers check the time on their phones, but fourteen-year-old Oscar Bell prefers clocks – old ones. He has twenty-three of them in his bedroom, and the oldest is from the nineteenth century.

Oscar became interested in clocks when he was nine. "My grandfather repaired clocks in his free time," he explains. "Every Saturday morning I went to his house and watched him work. He let me help with the small parts." When his grandfather stopped working two years ago, he gave Oscar all his tools.

Now Oscar repairs clocks for people in his town. He works on them at the weekend and for an hour every evening after he finishes his homework. "I never work on weekdays before school," he says. "I'm too sleepy in the morning, and you have to be very careful."

His bedroom can be a noisy place. "At midnight, about ten clocks ring at the same moment," he laughs. "My mum said it was terrible, so now I turn off the bells at night. My little sister liked them, though."

Last month a woman brought him a clock that stopped working fifty years ago. It took Oscar three weeks to repair it. "When she heard it again, she cried," he says. "That was the best moment of my year."

Oscar wants to open his own shop one day. "People think clocks are old-fashioned," he says, "but every home needs one."

part4.title: Why does a week have seven days?
part4.text:
People have {19} time in days, months and years for thousands of years. Days and years come from the sun, and months come from the moon. But where does the seven-day week come from?

About 4,000 years ago, people in Babylon {20} the sky every night. They could see seven big lights moving across it: the sun, the moon and five planets. They decided to give each day the name of one of these lights.

Later, the idea {21} to other countries. In English, some days still have these old names. Sunday is the sun's day and Monday is the moon's day. Saturday comes from the planet Saturn.

Not every country used a seven-day week. In Ancient Egypt, a week was ten days long. In France, at the end of the eighteenth century, the government {22} people to use a ten-day week too. But people didn't like it because they only had one day off {23} ten. The French ten-day week {24} for only about twelve years.

part7.model: One morning Hannah woke up and looked at her clock. It was eight o'clock! She thought she was late for school, so she got dressed quickly and ran out of the house with a piece of toast. When she arrived at school, the gate was closed. Then she remembered that it was Saturday!

items.q: What time does the girl's swimming lesson start?

script.t: Dad, what time is my swimming lesson tomorrow? Four o'clock, like last week?
No, the pool has changed the times. It starts at half past four now.
So we can leave home at four?
Yes. And it finishes at five, so I'll pick you up then.

items.q: When is the boy's birthday party?

script.t: Is your birthday party on Friday, Tom? That's your real birthday, isn't it?
Yes, but everyone has school the next day, so it's not then.
Saturday, then?
My cousins can't come on Saturday, so we're having it on Sunday afternoon.

items.q: What did the girl buy?

script.t: Did you buy a new watch at the shopping centre? Yours is broken.
I looked, but they were all too expensive. I got an alarm clock instead. I'm always late for school!
Good idea. Did you get a diary for next year too?
No, I'll ask for one for Christmas.

items.q: Which month is the school trip to the castle?

script.t: When's the school trip to the castle? Is it in June?
That's what Mr Lee said at first, but we have exams then. So it's in April now.
Oh. I thought it was after the summer holidays.
No, that's the trip to the museum, in October.

items.q: How long does the boy usually spend on homework every day?

script.t: How much homework do you do every day, Kai? Two hours?
No way! That's what my sister does. She's in her last year at school.
So less than that?
Usually about an hour. Thirty minutes is enough for maths, but then I need the same again for English.

part2.intro: You will hear a teacher telling students about a summer holiday club.
part2.title: Summer Holiday Activity Club

items.label: Bring every day: lunch, water bottle and a

script.t: Hello, everyone. I'm going to tell you about this year's Summer Holiday Activity Club. School finishes on Friday the eighteenth of July, and the club starts the next Monday – that's the twenty-first. It runs for two weeks, every weekday. Please don't come too early. The doors open at a quarter to nine every morning, and activities start at nine o'clock. We finish at three, not half past three like last year. Every day there are sports in the morning and art or music in the afternoon. There's also a special trip. Last year we went to the zoo on a Tuesday, but this year we're going to the beach, on the Thursday of the second week. The coach leaves at eight o'clock that day, so you'll need to come early. You'll need to bring lunch and a water bottle, and because it's summer, please bring a hat every day. We'll spend a lot of time outside. You don't need to bring sports clothes – just wear them. The club leader this year is Mrs Dawson. That's D-A-W-S-O-N. If you have any questions, you can email her before the end of June.

part3.intro: You will hear Lucy talking to her friend Nam about her new school.

items.q: Why does Lucy have to get up early?
options: Her new school is far from her home.
Lessons start at half past seven.

items.q: Why does Lucy like Wednesdays?
options: There is a meeting for students.

items.q: When does Lucy do her homework?
options: in the middle of the school day

items.q: What is Lucy's favourite subject now?
When will Lucy and Nam meet?

script.t: Hi Lucy. How's your new school? You look tired!
I am! I have to get up at six o'clock now. My old school was near my house, but this one is forty minutes away by bus.
Six! That's early. What time do lessons start?
At ten to eight. Lots of students arrive at half past seven to play football before school, but I'm never there that early.
And when do you finish?
Usually at four. But on Wednesdays we finish at half past two, because the teachers have a meeting. That's my favourite day of the week.
Do you get lots of homework?
Quite a lot. But I do it in the library at lunchtime, so I don't have to do it in the evening. Then I can watch TV or practise the guitar after dinner.
Good idea. What's your favourite lesson?

I thought it was going to be Art, because I loved it at my old school. But actually, it's History. The teacher tells us amazing stories about people from hundreds of years ago. Last week we learned about the fifteenth century.
Cool. Hey, are you free this weekend? We could go to the cinema on Saturday.
I'm visiting my aunt on Saturday. And on Sunday morning I'm going to sleep! But I'm free in the afternoon. Let's meet at three.
Perfect. See you on Sunday.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking to his mother.
items.q: Why was the boy late home?

script.t: Leo, it's nearly seven o'clock! Where were you?
Sorry, Mum. The football team had a meeting after lessons. The coach wanted to talk about next Saturday's match.
Why didn't you phone me?
My phone battery was dead. But I caught the first bus after the meeting, I promise!

script.t: Hi Jess, it's Ana. About tomorrow – I know we said we'd meet at the library at ten, but I've got a dentist's appointment at half past nine and I don't think I'll finish in time. Can we meet at eleven instead? Then we can still work on our project before lunch. Text me back. Bye!

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a new watch.
items.q: What does the girl think about her new watch?
options: It is difficult to see the time.

script.t: Nice watch, Mai. Is it new?
Yes, it was a birthday present from my uncle. It's a lovely colour, and it's not heavy at all.
Can you go swimming with it?
Yes. But the problem is the numbers. They're so small that I can never see what time it is! I always have to ask someone.

items.intro: You will hear a teacher talking to her class.
items.q: What is the teacher talking about?
options: the start time of a competition
a change to the holiday dates

script.t: Listen, everyone, I've got some news. The October holidays will start a week later than we said. That's because the swimming competition is now on the twentieth of October, and many of you are in the team. So your last day of school before the holidays is Friday the twenty-fourth, not the seventeenth. Please tell your parents tonight.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking about what he does on Sundays.
items.q: How does the boy feel about getting up early on Sundays?
options: He thinks it is too difficult.
He is worried about feeling tired at school.

script.t: Every Sunday I help my uncle at his bakery. I have to get up at five o'clock in the morning, when it's still dark. My friends think I'm crazy, and at first I really hated it. But now I love it. The streets are so quiet, and the bread smells amazing. And I finish at noon, so I have the whole afternoon free.

part5.intro: You will hear Sophie talking to her dad about next week. What will Sophie do on each day?

script.t: Sophie, let's write next week in the diary on the fridge. It's going to be a busy week.
OK, Dad. Monday first. I usually play badminton on Mondays, but the sports hall is closed next week.
So what are you doing instead?
My guitar teacher can't come on Thursday as usual, so she's moved my lesson to Monday at five.
Fine. Tuesday – that's your appointment with the dentist, isn't it? At quarter past four.
Yes. I wanted to go to homework club that day, but I can go the week after.
And Wednesday? There's swimming after school.
That's right. We're practising for the competition, so I can't miss it.
Then Thursday. No guitar, so you're free?
Not really. I've joined the cooking club. We're making pizza this week!
Great – bring some home! And Friday? Your friends asked about the cinema.
They want to see a film on Friday evening, but it's Grandma's birthday, and we're all having dinner at her house.
Of course! I nearly forgot. Let's go to the cinema on Saturday instead.
